Flu Outbreak in 2018 Disrupted South Africa’s Automotive Workforce

An influenza outbreak in early 2018 caused significant disruption to South Africa’s automotive industry, temporarily halting operations at key manufacturing sites across the Eastern Cape and Gauteng. While the sector has since recovered, industry stakeholders recently reflected on the scale and impact of the incident.

The outbreak, which peaked in late May 2018, affected hundreds of workers at several major plants, including those operated by Mzansi Motors and TransAfrica Auto. According to the National Automotive Employers' Association (NAEA), absenteeism rates in some facilities reached 40 percent at the height of the crisis, forcing companies to suspend production lines for up to a week.

"The health and safety of our workforce was the priority," said Sipho Dlamini, spokesperson for Mzansi Motors. "We had to close two of our assembly lines for four days to contain the spread and thoroughly sanitise the premises. It was a difficult but necessary measure."

The temporary closures resulted in an estimated loss of over 3,500 vehicles in output, with knock-on effects throughout the supply chain. Local suppliers faced cancelled orders and delivery delays, and export schedules were disrupted for several weeks as the plants worked to catch up on missed production.

Union representatives have described 2018 as "one of the most challenging years" for workers in the sector. "Some members were seriously ill and a few required hospitalisation," said Lerato Moeketsi of the South African Motor Industry Workers’ Union. "The outbreak exposed gaps in workplace health protocols and prompted a review of sick leave policies."

Automotive analyst Johan van Wyk noted that the events of 2018 led to more robust health management strategies. "We saw companies improve on-site medical screening and invest in better ventilation and hygiene training," he said. "The lessons learned have helped the industry become more resilient to health risks."

By July 2018, production levels had returned to normal and no long-term damage to the sector’s output was recorded. Authorities and industry leaders have since praised the coordinated response that allowed the industry to recover swiftly from what was, at the time, an unprecedented health challenge.
